messages.body_plain:
On 06/26/2014 07:39 AM, M Art wrote:
> Dear all
>
> I am dealing with a huge model with more than 700 parameters, 146
> observed variables, 28 latent variables, one of them affecting all
> observed variables and the rest affecting only between 8 and 15
> variables, some latent variables are orthogonal and others can
> correlate, all variances fixed to 1, and a sample of 1500 data. After
> 3000 iterations and once the computation has used all my 8Gb! ram memory

I am not surprised. R (and lavaan) are very hungry for memory. Are you
dealing with categorical data? Or is everything continuous?

If you have categorical data, try using the current dev version
(0.5-17.697) which is already much more efficient for categorical data.

> I get the corresponding message and the result shows that for example
> residual variances of the observed variables exceed the initial
> variances and no regression coefficients at all (all 0). Is there a way
> to incorporate inequality restrictions on the residual variances, like
> they can´t exceed observed variances, as to fix the estimation process
> to a subset and by this trying to avoid my problem in the estimation
> (maybe this helps!)?

Well, ou can label all the residual variances, eg

item1 ~~ v1*item1

and then you can add inequality constraints, like:

v1 < 2.5

where '2.5' is, say, the initial variance.

But I don't think this will help a bit. I would break it down in smaller
pieces, estimate those pieces separately, and then use these values as
starting values for the larger model.

Yves.

I am afraid lavaan.survey is not able to help you (for now).

Kind regards,
Silke

messages.subject: Re: cross-culturall validity lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Yes, invariance will be important if you want to compare the values of model coefficients across groups, but *partial* measurement invariance van be sufficient?  You need 2 indicators per factor (including the reference variable, with loading fixed to 1) to be invariant, not all of them.  If you can find 2 where invariance holds, then you have a basis for comparing model parameter estimates across groups.  Look for Steenkamp and Baumgartner's classic 1998 or 1999 Journal of Consumer Research paper.
--Ed Rigdon

If you don't check each factor, then there might be differences in parameter estimates because of differences in mean or scale for factors not checked.  I can imagine a large model where interest centers on just a few paths, and where some factors in another part of the model are not involved in those paths.      Remember also that factor model results only apply within the context of a certain model.  If you evaluate each factor in a model by itself and get a certain result, there is no guarantee that you will get the same result once you bring the factors back together in a larger model.

I would be grateful for thoughts on the following issue.

Suppose I want to have a set exogenous variables to all be uncorrelated. Is there a way to easily do this?

I'm wondering if there is an easy way to say in the syntax something that means "don't correlate these variables with anything else."

Here is the context: suppose I create named errors for the variables so that I might, for example, model the errors directly. Take a simple three factor Holzinger and Swineford example. If I create named errors

E_x1 =~ 1*x1
x1 ~~ 0*x1

messages.body_plain:
Factor indeterminacy originates in the rank problem that is at the root of common factor analysis.  Say you have 4 observed variables loading on 1 common factor.  Then the covariance matrix of the observed variables has rank at most 4--there are at most 4 dimensions of information to be extracted.  The common factor model includes 1 common factor and 4 errors or specific factors, and all of these are independent, making 5 dimensions of information.  How do you turn 4 dimensions of empirical information into 5?  Make the 5 indeterminate.
     The best recent source on factor indeterminacy would be the discussion in Stan Mulaik's indispensible (2010, 2nd ed.) Foundations of Factor Analysis.  Most books on factor-based SEM, including Hoyle's Handbook of SEM are silent.
     Classic literature includes Louis Guttman's (1955) comprehensive paper:
     Guttman, Louis (1955), THE DETERMINACY OF FACTOR SCORE MATRICES WITH IMPLICATIONS FOR FIVE OTHER BASIC PROBLEMS OF COMMON-FACTOR THEORY, British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8(2), 55-81.

On 07/03/2014 04:49 PM, kke...@nd.edu wrote:
> Suppose I want to have a set exogenous variables to all be uncorrelated.
> Is there a way to easily do this?

If you are looking for an option/argument for doing this automatically: no.

> 1. I realize that I can fix the covariances I want to zero within the
> model syntax, but this can be a little tedious doing that variable by
> variable (for many exogenous variables that I don't want correlated).

But this is R! You can easily 'generate' (parts of) model syntax. It is
just generating strings. For example:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

vis <- paste0("visual ~~ ",  paste0("0*E_x", 1:9, collapse = " + "))
txt <- paste0("textual ~~ ", paste0("0*E_x", 1:9, collapse = " + "))
spd <- paste0("speed ~~ ",   paste0("0*E_x", 1:9, collapse = " + "))

ortho <- apply(combn(9,2), 2, function(x)
                paste0("E_x", x[1], " ~~ ", "0*E_x", x[2]))

errors <- paste0("E_x", 1:9, " =~ 1*x", 1:9, "; x", 1:9, " ~~ 0*x", 1:9)

and then, you glue them together:

fit <- cfa( c(HS.model, errors, vis, txt, spd, ortho),
data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

> 2. I also realize that I can use "orthogonal = TRUE" in, say, sem() to
> have *all* of the exogenous variables uncorrected (and allow specific
> correlations by explicitly specifying them in the lavaan syntax), but
> this doesn't seem ideal either.

What about the lavaan() function? Only the parameters you specify in the
model syntax will be estimated. Everything else is fixed to zero.

So, the above syntax would simplify to:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ 1*x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ 1*x7 + x8 + x9
               visual ~~ textual + speed
               textual ~~ speed '

errors <- paste0("E_x", 1:9, " =~ 1*x", 1:9, "; x", 1:9, " ~~ 0*x", 1:9)

fit <- lavaan(c(HS.model, errors), auto.var=TRUE,
data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

> I'm wondering if there is an easy way to say in the syntax something
> that means "don't correlate these variables with anything else."

No. Perhaps I could add a new operator. Something like

var1 + var2 + var3 + var4 ~~ 0

but we do not gain much.

Yves.

You are almost at the very minimum of this condition.  As a result, standard errors for the path estimates related to these higher order factors will be large, and confidence intervals will be wide.  It may be that the model is misspecified, but with parameter values just outside the acceptable range, I think that the weak identification is the more likely problem.
     If that is true, then you might address the problem by making the statistical identification more firm. That would mean either more dependents per factor, more correlates per factor, or (probably most effective) fewer free parameters.  If you have prior knowledge that would let you fix some of the parameter estimates to "known" values, then your other, free parameter estimates would become more stable, and you might obtain more acceptable estimates.
     You might also consider bootstrapping.  Perhaps if you re sample your data repeatedly, you will see that the mean values across replications are actually within the acceptable range.  That would be easy enough to set up and run.
--Ed Rigdon

> growth() function. In my model syntax, I've fixed the variances to be 1
> since I'm estimating thresholds.

No need to fix the variances, if you are using parameterization="delta"
(which is the default). lavaan will ignore the fixed values.

> that they're being estimated which makes no sense to me!

But they are NOT estimated. Their values are simply a deterministic
function of other model parameters. Note that they have no standard errors.

You can always 'check' the free/estimated model parameters by typing

inspect(fit)

Yves.

The core of the ESEM technique in Mplus is Bayesian relaxation of the strict CFA assumption that “all other loadings are fixed at 0.”  In ESEM, these other loadings are given prior distributions which may be centered on 0 but with small variances so that estimates in individual replications need not be 0 exactly.  Thus ESEM retains the prior information that links particular observed variables with particular factors and generally excludes other links, but with a Bayesian “fudge factor”

messages.body_plain:
I believe nearly the exact same exploratory design can be accomplished in the full information approach via IRT methods, which Seongho mentioned is possible with mirt. If you fit a confirmatory item factor analysis model and observe a poor fit (say via something like the M2 statistic, or similarly with lavaan's WLSMV approach) then you can free up additional slope/loading parameters to see if the fit improves. Improvement can be judged both from a likelihood ratio and model fit standpoint to see if estimating these additional parameters are really helpful.

However as you said --- and what appears to be the primary inspiration for ESEM in the first place --- is if there is a priori knowledge that these additional exploratory slopes should be close to zero then users can just include an informative Bayesian prior parameter distribution in the model estimation for these parameters (say, a Gaussian one with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of .2, or even stronger depending on the knowledge of the researcher). The same effect is achieved, and you get the so-called 'fudge factor' all while avoiding the ad-hoc rotation methodology implemented in Mplus. Plus, different priors and weights can be used for each parameter, so in that sense it may even be more flexible. So I think Seongho is correct in that respect. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
On 07/09/2014 10:59 PM, Cathy Zhang wrote:
> CFI. I noticed that under the "type" argument, we can implement yuan's
> method of bootstrap. In Yuan, Hayashi and Yanagihara (2007)'s original
> paper about this bootstrap method, it talks about bootstrapping RMSEA
> and how to set the population RMSEA to a specific population value. And
> indeed, bootstrapLavaan provides the option to set population RMSEA to a
> specific value using the "h0.RMSEA". My question is if we don't specify
> "h0.RMSEA", how does the function set the population RMSEA value?

I'm not sure. This was coded by Ed Merkle
(http://psychology.missouri.edu/merklee), so you may wish to contact him
for more details. But in the source code, so can see this:

   # Calculate tauhat_1, middle p. 267.
             # Yuan et al note that tauhat_1 could be negative;
             # if so, we need to let S.a = Sigmahat. (see middle p 275)
             ifelse(length(h0.rmsea)==0,
               tau.hat <- (ghat - df)/(n-1),  # middle p 267
               tau.hat <- df*(h0.rmsea^2))    # middle p 273

so if h0.rmsea is not provided, 'tau.hat' is computed as (ghat -
df)/(n-1), while if you do provide h0.rmsea, it is computed as
df*(h0.rmsea^2))

The page numbers refer to the 2007 paper. Hopefully this helps.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Edward,

Yes, your observation is right. The core of the ESEM technique in Mplus is a Bayesian relaxation of the strict CFA assumption, theoretically. In practical perspectives, CFA assumption is too strict to estimating loadings, Fit indices, and too high (overestimated) correlation between hypothesized factors for applied psychologists. So, I saw some researchers to want a more flexible estimation of their factor models to construct validation with the ESEM technique in Mplus.

I believe the "mirt" can reach the purpose of the ESEM technique. And I fully agree with Phil's opinion. If I'm the Mplus user, be naturally exultant over, I'll use the ESEM technique. Because, it's very convenient to find a number of factors or make rational arguments for my factor models for the Mplus users. But, I'm the R user. In the R packages, We already have an excellent package for estimating factor structure with exploratory and confirmatory design in the full information approach via IRT methods that is "mirt". It can be a good alternative Mplus which Phil already mentioned. Why we should use the ESEM technique in lavaan? I can agree implantation of the ESEM technique in the lavaan, but I recommend to use the "mirt" package until the state of the current development of the lavaan. The mirt package very useful to know state of Item response characteristic the each item. Knowing Item response characteristics very important in some research topics. Cheers.

Best wishes,
Seongho Bae.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

A quick question about obtaining standardized solutions for MGCFA models.

I have run a multi-group (2 countries, in my case) CFA on a 2-factor measurement scale. In my analysis, I have constrained the intercepts and loadings to be equal across groups. The model fit is fine, and the estimated (unstandardized) intercepts and loadings are indeed equivalent across groups.

However, my co-authors and I would like to report the standardized solution (the column "Std.all" in the output) and I notice that these are not identical across groups. There is clearly something I'm not understanding about the way the standardized estimates are computed.

Can anyone provide some insight as to why the standardized solution (but not the non-standardized solution) differs across groups? It seems that, if I can't report the standardized solution, I'd be better off to provide the non-standardized estimates.

I'm pasting below a reproducible example using the Holzinger Swineford data that comes with the lavaan package. Running this model gives the the same situation as running the model on my own data- the non-standardized loadings and intercepts are identical across groups, but the standardized solutions are different across groups.

HS.model <- ' visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <-  cfa(HS.model,
 data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
 group = "school",
 group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))

summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

Many thanks in advance for any insight that anyone could provide.

Best,
M Friedman

messages.subject: Re: Question on Latent Variable Indicators
messages.body_plain:
In factor analysis, latent variables do not have any scale. Users should define their scaling of their latent variables. The methods of the scale specification could be by using marker variable, fixing the scale of factor (e.g., mean of 0 and variance of 1), or effect coding method. You can search it in all introduction to SEM book.

However, there is a problem if you use indicators with largely different scales. I believe it is the problem of computer algorithm. The inversion of the matrix or eigenvalue decomposition could have a problem. I would recommend you to rescale some of you indicators by dividing it by an appropriate constant.

y11 ~~ var1*y11

messages.subject: RE: Question on Latent Variable Indicators
messages.body_plain:
TRM—

     In a simple case of a single group and a well-fitting model, the differences are a matter of the unstandardized parameter estimates.  Remember that the formula for a simple regression coefficient is:

b = covariance (X,Y) / variance (X)

So anything that affects the variance of X or the covariance of X and Y (two factors, say) will affect the value of b.  You can also write this as:

b = correlation(X,Y) x stdev(Y) / stdev(X)

if that clarifies the impact of the scale of Y and X on b.

     So if we directly set the variance of factor X or factor Y to a different value, we also set stdev(X) or stdev(Y) and thus affect b.

     For the other approach, assume we have an exclusive reflective indicator of factor X, called x1, and the equation is:

x1 = 0 + loading x X + e

So I am setting the intercept for x1 to 0.  Otherwise, the arithmetic is more involved.  If factor X and e are orthogonal (the usual regression assumption), then we also have:

Variance(x1) = loading ^2 x variance(X) + variance(e)

If we fix this loading to 1, then it becomes:

Variance(x1) = variance(X) + variance(e)

Which also implies:

Variance(X) = variance(x1) - variance(e)

Now variance(x1) is fixed in the data.  So fixing the loading to 1 constraints variance(X) to be the difference between variance(x1) and variance(e).  If different indicators have different variances, or even just different error variances, then setting different loadings to 1 will lead to different variances for the factor.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: random crashes under windows: fixed
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Cc: Lisa, Oscar

Both Lisa and Oscar have reported 'random' crashes of lavaan; see:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/8ncLFuKYzuE
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/O7GIIqMeIGc

These crashes have haunted me for several weeks now. They only occurred under windows (not linux or mac osx), typically when running a simulation study using categorical data. I was pretty sure that lavaan was innocent (since it is written in R without any compiled code), but I needed to be 100% sure. Perhaps, one of the external packages (e.g. pbivnorm was the culprit. But after a *long* time of testing/debugging, I was able to trace back these crashes to ... the nlminb() function (which is part of the stats package in R). Once I could create a small reproducible script, I filed an official bug report to the R developers (see https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=15914). They discovered that the bug was in fact due to an optimization bug in the gcc compiler for windows. But Duncan Murdoch provided a workaround, and this is now fixed in the dev version of R, which you can install from here: http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/rdevel.html . This version will eventually become R 3.2.0

In the meantime,  if you experience these crashes, you can circumvent the problem by installing the dev version of lavaan (0.5-17.701 or higher) and using control=list(cor.optim.method="BFGS") or control=list(cor.optim.method="optimize"), to change the optimizer needed for computing the polychoric correlations. For the lavPredict() function, we added the argument optim.method, so you can now use lavPredict(fit, optim.method = "BFGS"). But the nlminb() optimizer works (slightly) better (and faster), so installing the dev version of R is perhaps the better solution.

And so, now this is fixed, I can finally sleep well again.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Exogenous variables are the variables that are not predicted by any other variables in the model. For example, in

'y ~ x1 + x2'

x1 and x2 are exogenous variables. lavaan provides two methods to use maximum likelihood. First, it treats x1 and x2 as exogenous variables like multiple regression. The distributions of x1 and x2 are not assumed. However, the parameters only relating x1 and x2 cannot be estimated, such as variance of x1, covariance between x1 and x2, or mean of x2. This method is good if you do not want to assume normal distribution on x1 and x2 and x1 and x2 do not have missing data. This is the default option of lavaan. Second, it treats x1 and x2 as endogenous variables so x1 and x2 are assumed to be normally distributed. The distribution of x1, x2, and y are estimated simultaneously. You can estimate any parameters relating to x1 and x2 but it assumes normal distribution. You may use this option by specifying fixed.x = FALSE. For example,

sem(myModel, myData, fixed.x = FALSE)
